questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a perianal lesion. He was known to have HIV infection (last CD4 count of 20 cells/μL, HIV-RNA viral load of 1.2 million). The lesion had been present for over 2.5 years and had previously responded to aciclovir or valaciclovir but had never completely healed. On this occasion, the painful ulcer had not responded to a 10-day course of oral valaciclovir 1 gram twice daily followed by a 14-day course of oral aciclovir 400 mg three times a day that was prescribed at the local STD clinic. The patient reported adherence to both regimens. DNA sequencing for resistance mutations cannot be obtained.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: IV foscarnet The patient is likely infected with a thymidine kinase (TK)deficient virus, and the virus is resistant to high-dose aciclovir, valaciclovir, famciclovir, ganciclovir, or valganciclovir. Foscarnet is the drug of choice in thymidine kinase-deficient HSV . Alternatively, cidofovir can also be used, but it is much more nephrotoxic than foscarnet. Topical compound cidofovir creams can also be used, but this is not commercially available. Ribavirin has no activity against the herpes viruses.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q7

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of worsening headache. She had no past medical history of note but worked as an air hostess. Recent flights had been to New York, Los Angeles, and Paris. She was married with one teenage son and had not had any new sexual partners. She did not have any oral or genital ulceration on specific questioning. She had had similar illnesses on at least two other occasions. On examination she was photophobic with mild neck stiffness. She was alert and cognitively intact. Investigations: Peripheral white cell count 7.1 ×109/L CSF white cell count 342 ×106/L; 99% lymphocytes CSF protein 1012 mg/L CSF/plasma glucose 2.6/5.2 mmol/L CSF microscopy: no organisms seen
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: HSV-2 Aseptic meningitis may be caused by HSV , enterovirus, CMV , and B. burgdorferi; however, the recurrent nature of the episodes of meningitis make this much more likely to be HSV-2. Recurrent meningococcal infections are recognized and occur due to a terminal complement deficiency; however, the CSF profile does not fit, she is older than would be expected for an inherited complement deficiency, and she has no risk factors for an acquired deficiency. Neuroborreliosis may present with an acute or chronic meningitis, but recurrent episodes would be unusual. HSV-2 meningitis may present in the absence of genital lesions; humans are the only known reservoir, but the vast majority of genital HSV infections are unrecognized (approx. 85%–90%). The first episode of HSV-2 meningitis usually occurs within 2 weeks of primary genital HSV infection. It is more common in women than men. The incidence of recurrent meningitis is reported to be around 30%. Lack of prior HSV-1 infection may predispose to more symptomatic HSV-2 infection, both genital and meningeal.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q11

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man presented with new penile lesions. He had insertive vaginal and oral intercourse using a latex condom with a casual female partner 72 hours earlier. He denied any current medications, known past medical history, or allergies. He was a college student and worked parttime in a chemistry laboratory. On examination, there were erythematous plaques over the shaft and glans penis.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Psoriasis Genital psoriasis can cause significant distress and is often confused with sexually transmitted infections. It has been estimated that the first presentation of psoriasis is genital in as many as 2%–5% of cases, making it a diagnosis that Infectious Disease clinicians may encounter. The lesions develop due to the Koebner phenomenon or “isomorphic response,” which describes the development of skin lesions in sites of skin trauma (in this case friction associated with coitus) that may be seen in psoriasis. There is no history of latex allergy in the setting of likely prior contact (“works in a laboratory,” no history of food allergies), nor are the lesions or time course a good fit for primary syphilis, HIV , or HSV .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q48

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presented with a new genital rash. The lesions were associated with mild burning. She had a history of orolabial cold sores. She and her male sex partner of 2 years reported no other concurrent sex partners. They used barrier contraception with condoms, and she was taking the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination, a vulvar rash was observed
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: New acquisition of HSV-2 Symptoms associated with HSV-2 infection vary wildly. Primary episode outbreaks are associated with initial infection and are typically more severe than recurrences. Nonprimary first episode of genital herpes (i.e., in a patient who already has oral herpes as this patient does) may be less severe or asymptomatic. Typically there are fewer lesions and fewer systemic symptoms. In patients presenting with lesions concerning for genital herpes, HSV-2 and HSV-1 NAAT or culture should be performed on specimens obtained from the lesion(s). Concurrently serologic testing should be performed. Positive culture or NAAT without antibody is consistent with recent infection. Positive culture with antibody is consistent with longer infection. Testing her current partner might be helpful but if he were positive, it would not delineate whether she acquired HSV from him. The rash will spontaneously resolve. However, it may recur. Latex allergies are less likely to present with localized findings like this. T. pallidum is possible but typically presents with one ulcer and most often without itching or pain. (Image from Patel R. Genital herpes. Medicine, 2014;42(7),354–358.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q10

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presented with headache, agitation, and delirium. She had a witnessed generalized seizure in the emergency department. She was started on antiepileptic medication, and head CT was performed to evaluate for stroke. The head CT was within normal limits. Brain MRI was later performed, and it demonstrated bilateral temporal lobe enhancement.
questions.lead_in: What test would be most likely to prove the correct diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CSF HSV PCR This patient likely has HSV-1 encephalitis. Disproportionate enhancement of the temporal lobes, as demonstrated on her MRI, is characteristic. Behavioral abnormalities and new-onset seizures are also common.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q31

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with acute unilateral vision loss. On funduscopic examination, he has significant vitreitis and retinal findings concerning for acute retinal necrosis.
questions.explanation: Aciclovir Acute retinal necrosis is most often caused by varicella zoster virus, and therapy with aciclovir should be administered. Corticosteroids may be used to decrease ocular inflammation but should not be given until after antiviral therapy is initiated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q30

questions.question: Neonatal herpes

parts.text: What are the three possible clinical syndromes
What are the % vertical transmission during a primary infection episode and during a reactivation episode?
What is the management of the following women: Term woman with active recurrence lesions?
What is the management of the following women: Term woman without active lesions with primary infection at 32 weeks?
What is the management of the following women: Woman with recurrent lesions (did not mention which trimester)?

cohort_answer.text:
Three clinical syndromes: Skin, eye and mucuous membrane infection; Localized central nervous system; Disseminated
% vertical transmission: Primary: up to 60% (as per CPS statement); First episode non-primary: ≤30%; Recurrent: <2%
Term with active recurrence lesions: C-section
Women with primary genital herpes in the third trimester of pregnancy have a high risk of transmitting HSV to their neonates and should be counselled accordingly and should be offered a Caesarean section to decrease this risk. Can be placed on ppx 36 weeks onwards.
Woman with recurrent lesions: Treatment for active episode, then offered acyclovir or valacyclovir suppression at 36 weeks' gestation to decrease the risk of clinical lesions and viral shedding at the time of delivery and therefore decrease the need for Caesarean section.

questions.question: [image-based question: Photo given of nurse working in ICU who comes in with meningeal symptoms and vesicles at various stages on the inner thigh and right labia.]

parts.text: What is the most likely diagnosis and pathogen?
Describe the pathogenesis in 4 steps.
What are four neurological complications.
Can the patient return to work and when?

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Genital HSV (Redbook: HSV infection also can manifest as mild, self-limited aseptic meningitis, usually associated with genital HSV-2 infection; ~25% of primary HSV2 can have aseptic meningitis). Pathogenesis: Most viral pathogens affecting the CNS initially infect mucosal surfaces followed by viral replication in regional lymph nodes; subsequently, primary viremia that signals the onset of illness and subsequent seeding of other organs; except for neonatal HSV infection, most viruses reach the CNS during a second viremia that follows viral replication in other organs, particularly the liver and spleen. Neurological complications: Transverse myelitis; Encephalitis; Bell's palsy; Ascending myelitis; Mollaret meningitis (recurrent aseptic meningitis); Acute retinal necrosis. Return to work: Transmission of HSV infection from health care professionals with genital lesions is not likely as long as they comply with hand hygiene policies; can return to work once well

questions.question: Neonatal HSV

parts.text: Name 3 clinical manifestations in neonatal HSV
Transmission risk for: Asymptomatic neonate born vaginally to mother with HSV primary infx (doesn’t say when she had infx)
Transmission risk for: Asymptomatic neonate born c/s to mother with recurrent infx
Transmission risk for: Septic looking baby, can’t recall what stage mother had

questions.model_answer: a) Three clinical manifestations of neonatal HSV: (1) Skin-eye-mouth (SEM) disease. (2) CNS disease (encephalitis). (3) Disseminated disease (multi-organ involvement including liver, lung, adrenal). b) Asymptomatic neonate, vaginal delivery, mother with primary infection (timing unspecified, assume near delivery): high transmission risk, approximately 25-60% (commonly cited up to 50%) if primary infection is active at time of delivery. c) Asymptomatic neonate, C-section, mother with recurrent infection: low risk, less than 1-2% (recurrent infection has lower viral shedding and C-section further reduces exposure). d) Septic-appearing baby (disseminated neonatal HSV, maternal infection stage unclear): treat empirically regardless of exact transmission risk stratification - high mortality if untreated (~30% even treated for disseminated disease); start IV acyclovir immediately.

parts.text: What is the risk of neonatal HSV transmission for a primary herpes outbreak?

questions.model_answer: a) Transmission risk, primary outbreak: approximately 25-60% (commonly quoted up to 50%) with vaginal exposure to active primary lesions. b) Transmission risk, recurrent disease: low, approximately 1-3% (lower viral shedding, presence of maternal antibody). c) Neonatal drug: acyclovir 60 mg/kg/day IV divided q8h (20 mg/kg IV q8h), for 14 days (SEM disease) or 21 days (CNS/disseminated disease). d) Sites to swab for HSV testing (4): conjunctivae/eyes, mouth/oropharynx, nasopharynx, and skin/rectum (surface culture/PCR from mucocutaneous sites), plus blood and CSF PCR. e) Three congenital/neonatal HSV syndromes and treatment duration: (1) Skin-eye-mouth (SEM) disease - IV acyclovir x14 days. (2) CNS disease (encephalitis) - IV acyclovir x21 days. (3) Disseminated disease - IV acyclovir x21 days (all followed by suppressive oral acyclovir x6 months in survivors).

questions.question: What would you do in the following scenarios: mother in labor with active primary genital herpes? Mother in labor with primary herpes at 32 weeks gestation no active lesions at present?

parts.text: Mother in labor with primary herpes at 32 weeks gestation no active lesions at present, what would you do?
For mother/baby with active primary genital herpes in labor, what would you do?
b) Mother with recurrent herpes during pregnancy? What is the risk of HSV infection in infant?
For baby if symptomatic, treatment durations

cohort_answer.text:
If no current active lesions: advise/discuss C-section; swab baby mucous membranes within 24hrs of delivery for HSV PCR; send baby home if doing well while awaiting PCR; if symptoms or PCR+ then re-admit and start Acyclovir, get blood/CSF PCR; if blood/CSF positive Acyclovir x21 days, if negative x14d
For mother: assess for active lesions/prodromal symptoms; if present offer C-section ASAP; if absent discuss risk/benefit of C-section; avoid/limit scalp electrodes. For baby: vaginal delivery, swab and NAT blood/CSF at delivery; treat with Acyclovir while awaiting testing if mom has lesions; if asymptomatic no treatment/no routine swabs, educate parents
Recurrent HSV: if lesions present 2-5%, if no lesions 0.02-0.05%. Non-primary first genital episode: <30%. Primary infection, particularly late in pregnancy: 30-60%. Risk factors: nature of infection (primary ~60%, recurrent <2%), mode of delivery, duration of ROM, intrapartum instrumentation, neonatal factors. Maternal prophylaxis with valacyclovir/acyclovir from 36 weeks until delivery for recurrent infection
If LP+ or blood+: treat 21 days minimum IV acyclovir. If blood/CSF negative but swabs positive: 14 days. If all negative: 10 days if high risk. Repeat LP near end of 21 days for CNS disease. Ophthalmology check, trifluridine if ocular infection. CNS/disseminated HSV after negative LP - switch to oral suppressive acyclovir for 6 months

questions.question: ICU RN with herpetic lesions on inner thigh (photo shown) and labia majora presents with lymphocytic meningitis.

parts.text: What is the diagnosis and pathogen?
4 steps in the pathogenesis of her CNS infection
Name 4 other neurologic complications of this organism.
Can she go back to work? Justify your answer

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: HSV-2 meningitis (recurrence = Mollaret's); treat only if immunosuppressed (acyclovir 10mg/kg IV q8h or valacyclovir 500mg PO BID x7 days); can offer suppressive therapy. Pathogenesis: viral contact with mucosa/broken skin and replication at site; retrograde ascension up sensory neuron to dorsal root ganglion establishing latency; reactivation causes anterograde travel to site near primary infection; virus can travel across synapses into CNS causing meningitis/encephalitis. Other complications: Encephalitis, Transverse myelitis, Trigeminal neuralgia (HSV-1), Post-infectious encephalomyelitis, Peripheral neuritis, Temporal lobe epilepsy. Return to work: Yes - initially needs contact/droplet until etiology confirmed by PCR, then can resume work with lesions covered; viral meningitis (adult) routine precautions, (peds) contact until enterovirus ruled out

parts.text: What are 3 clinical syndromes of HSV in neonate? What is risk transmission to baby if mother has first primary HSV during pregnancy? If recurrent HSV during pregnancy? Mother in labour without rupture membranes, has active lesions, how do you manage mom? Mother in labour at 32 weeks, had primary HSV during 3rd trimester no active lesions, how do you manage mom? Mother has history recurrent HSV none currently, how do you manage?

cohort_answer.text:
SEM - skin, eyes, mucous membranes (tx 14 days), 45%, high risk progression if untreated, anytime before 6 weeks. Localized CNS HSV (tx 21 days), 30%, usually 2nd-3rd week of life (up to 6 weeks). Disseminated HSV (tx 21 days), sepsis-like with end organ involvement (liver, lungs, CNS, heart, adrenals, bone marrow, renal, GI, skin). Intra-uterine HSV (<5%, very rare)
Primary HSV 25-60% (60% if primary infection at time of birth). First episode non-primary <30%. Recurrent infection <2%. Presents within 6 weeks of life
Women with active lesions or prodrome at delivery should be offered elective C/S. If ROM occurs, C/S ideally within 4 hours. If delivery imminent, no benefit to C/S. Contact precautions for mom during labor, delivery, postpartum
Woman with primary HSV any time during 3rd trimester -> C/S recommended (ACOG and RCOG UK)
Offer suppressive antiviral at or beyond 36 weeks gestation (acyclovir or valacyclovir); C/S not required; avoid scalp electrodes/fetal scalp monitoring/vacuum/forceps if possible. Infant: observe for signs of NHSV, does not require ACV therapy, mucous membrane swabs not routinely recommended

questions.question:
Q9 (2016 AM) Viral meningitis
26F who is an ICU nurse develops headache, photophobia and on examination has lesions on her thigh and right labia (shown picture of a crop of vesicles). CSF shows 17 WBC (95% lymphocytes) with elevated protein

parts.text: A) What is the diagnosis and the pathogen responsible (be specific)
B) Explain the pathogenesis of CNS infection
C) Can she return to work and justify your answer
D) Four other neuro manifestations of her condition

cohort_answer.text:
A) HSV-2 meningitis. Viral meningitis in immunocompetent adults is generally caused by HSV-2. Genital lesions present in 85% of patients with primary HSV-2 meningitis and precede onset of CNS sx by 7 days. CSF profile: pleocytosis with predominance of lymphocytes, normal glucose.

B) HSV invades through peripheral nerves (sacral nerves in this case). Once within the CNS, viruses spread through the subarachnoid space in CSF, causing an inflammatory response leading to meningitis; may also spread directly or via inflammatory leukocytes through neural tissue to neurons and glial cells. Viruses enter the CNS via: (1) haematogenous spread after replicating outside the CNS (e.g. enteroviruses), crossing the blood-brain barrier directly or carried in infected leukocytes (mumps, measles, herpesviruses), infecting vascular endothelial cells - note HSV-2 viraemia is common in primary infection; (2) invasion through peripheral and cranial nerves (as for polio and HSV respectively).

C) Yes - HCWs with genital HSV infection do not have to inform OHS of these conditions. There should be no risk to patients as long as good hygiene is maintained, including meticulous hand hygiene, and lesions are covered.

D) Recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis (Mollaret's meningitis) - transient neurological manifestations including seizures, hallucinations, diplopia, cranial nerve palsies, or altered consciousness in half of patients. Sacral Radiculopathy (Elsberg syndrome) - affects lumbar/sacral nerve roots, often recurrent, with radicular pain, paresthesias, urinary retention, constipation, anogenital discomfort, leg weakness. Bell's Palsy. Transverse myelitis (not encephalitis - that is mostly caused by HSV-1).

questions.question:
Q29 (2014)
Herpes simplex virus

parts.text: A. 4 neurologic complications:
B. most common mechanism of resistance to acyclovir:

cohort_answer.text:
A: Aseptic meningitis (HSV1 and HSV2). Mollaret's meningitis (HSV-2). Encephalitis (HSV-1). Transverse myelitis (HSV-2 and 1). Sacral radiculitis (HSV-2, with acute urinary retention called Elsberg syndrome, extremely rare). Acute retinal necrosis (HSV-1?). Cranial neuropathy (HSV-1 - Bell's palsy)

B: Thymidine kinase mutations (90-95% of Acyclovir resistance). Acyclovir must be phosphorylated first by the viral thymidine kinase (TK) and then by cellular kinases before inhibiting the virus-encoded DNA polymerase (DNA pol). Resistant HSV infection usually characterized by a chronic, progressive ulcerative mucocutaneous disease with prolonged shedding of virus in immunocompromised hosts

questions.question: HSV Infection:

parts.text: A) Mutations to what two proteins can cause Acyclovir Resistance?
B) For a swab from a vesicle, what are two tests other than PCR that can make a diagnosis of HSV?

questions.model_answer: a) Two proteins with mutations causing acyclovir resistance: (1) Viral thymidine kinase (TK) - most common mechanism, reduced/absent phosphorylation of acyclovir to active form. (2) Viral DNA polymerase - less common, alters acyclovir triphosphate binding site. b) Two tests other than PCR for HSV diagnosis from a vesicle swab: (1) Viral culture (cell culture with cytopathic effect, historically gold standard though less sensitive than PCR). (2) Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) staining or Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells - less specific/sensitive but rapid).

questions.question: Q75 2023 Day 1. Acyclovir.

parts.text: 2 viral enzyme mutations associated with resistance
EBV 4 malignancies (2022)

cohort_answer.text:
2 viral enzyme mutations: Thymidine Kinase - absent/low production of viral thymidine kinase, or altered TK substrate specificity (thymidine >>> acyclovir). Viral DNA Polymerase - altered viral DNA polymerase (UL54).
EBV malignancies: Burkitt Lymphoma; B-Cell Lymphoma; DLBCL; Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma; Hodgkin Lymphoma; Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma; Gastric Lymphoma; T-cell Lymphoma; Primary CNS Lymphoma (PCNSL).
